Taxi Association calls for permanent fare review, seeks retention of interim rate
item.description: The Fiji Taxi Association has criticised the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission’s decision to end the interim taxi fare adjustment on 30th September and return the distance rate to $1 per kilometre from 1st October 2026. Association President Mohammed Faiyaz says many taxi operators are struggling to earn enough to replace ageing vehicles or invest in safer and better-quality taxis.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Taxi Association has criticised the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission’s decision to end the interim taxi fare adjustment on 30th September and return the distance rate to $1 per kilometre from 1st October 2026.

Association President Mohammed Faiyaz says many taxi operators are struggling to earn enough to replace ageing vehicles or invest in safer and better-quality taxis.

Faiyaz says the FCCC must reverse the decision and commence an urgent permanent fare review.

He stresses that a 2011 distance rate has no place in Fiji in 2026.

The Association says it had sought a permanent and comprehensive fare review and proposed a distance rate of $1.50 per kilometre.

Faiyaz says operators are also facing higher costs for tyres, batteries, engine oil, vehicle parts, servicing, mechanical labour, insurance, financing and replacement vehicles.

He says the $1 per kilometre distance rate was established in 2011 and does not reflect the current cost of operating a taxi.

Faiyaz says while flagfall and waiting charges were adjusted in 2022, the core distance rate remained unchanged.

He says petrol was approximately $2.33 per litre and diesel approximately $2.02 per litre in 2011, compared with $3.06 for petrol and $2.92 for diesel on Viti Levu following the latest reduction.

The Association says operators paid approximately $50 each to recalibrate their meters and will now have to spend about another $50 to return their meters to the old rate.

It says operators could also lose working hours while waiting for their meters to be recalibrated because of the limited number of authorised meter service providers.

The Association is questioning who will reimburse operators for the further recalibration costs and lost working hours.

It says affordable public transport should not come at the expense of individual taxi owners and drivers and is calling for the current fare to continue until a permanent review is completed.

item.title: Balancing motherhood and public service is one of my biggest challenges- Bainivalu
item.description: Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu says her most important job begins when she gets home to her children. Speaking about her experience as a Member of Parliament, Bainivalu says balancing her responsibilities as a Minister and a mother has been one of the biggest challenges of her political career.
item.content:encoded:
Minister for Fisheries and Forestry Alitia Bainivalu says her most important job begins when she gets home to her children.

Speaking about her experience as a Member of Parliament, Bainivalu says balancing her responsibilities as a Minister and a mother has been one of the biggest challenges of her political career.

She says once she returns home from work, her focus shifts to caring for her children, helping them with homework and making sure they are looked after , often making it difficult to attend community meetings in the evenings.

Bainivalu says this is a challenge many male parliamentarians may not experience in the same way.

She believes more women should support one another if Fiji is to see greater female representation in Parliament.

Bainivalu notes that although women made up a large proportion of voters in the last General Election, only five women were elected to Parliament.

She says political parties should also consider increasing the number of women candidates to improve female representation.

Bainivalu is encouraging women interested in politics to enter public service with a genuine desire to help others, saying being a Member of Parliament is a calling to serve the people.

item.title: From 20 Cents to a Doctor-Dr Tukaha Mua
item.description: With 20 cents in his pocket, Doctor Alfred Tukaha Mua left his home in Malha'a, Rotuma to pursue his secondary school at Queen Victoria School with a promise in mind never to go hungry and live in poverty again. This was shared by his daughter Makereta Mua during the launching of his book The Head of the Table at the Tanoa Hotel in Suva.
item.content:encoded:
With 20 cents in his pocket, Doctor Alfred Tukaha Mua left his home in Malha'a, Rotuma to pursue his secondary school at Queen Victoria School with a promise in mind never to go hungry and live in poverty again.

This was shared by his daughter Makereta Mua during the launching of his book The Head of the Table at the Tanoa Hotel in Suva.

She says at thirteen years old, her father said goodbye to his family and the familiar surroundings of Malha'a, Rotuma and was leaving behind the place he called home, the people he loved, and the simple island life he had always known.

Mua says that when he began his journey to Fiji, her father had very little in his possession and there was no guarantee of what lay ahead—only 20 cents and a heart filled with hope.

Mua stressed that what mattered was the determination he carried within him.

The daughter says her father knew that his journey to Queen Victoria School was more than just a journey to continue his education; it was the beginning of a new chapter in his life, and he was determined to make something of himse lf and to build a future different from the hardships he had known.

Many doctors and nurses families, friends and people from the medical field attended the launching tonight.
